evidence.quote: Lemons – Grow well in warmer areas.  Adaptable to different areas.  HU 1100 to 1500. Main crop in hotter areas produced in February to March, while crop in cooler areas produced during May to July.

harvestMonths.notes: Two sub-regions in one source: hot areas (main crop Feb-Mar) and cooler KZN areas (main crop May-Jul). Months listed combine both: [2,3] hot area main crop, [5,6,7] cooler area main crop.

harvestMonths.region: South Africa (general; main areas Eastern Cape, Limpopo, Western Cape)

evidence.quote: Eureka lemons can have as much as three fruit sets. This means that at the same time there can be as much as three lots of fruit on a tree that are at different stages of maturity. Because of this characteristic, trees can produce marketable fruit from as early as February in hotter areas, and to as late as mid-September in cooler regions.
evidence.doc: Citrus Growers' Association / Citrus Academy — 'Citrus Planting Management 2: Citrus Types and Cultivars' Learner Guide (1st edition), Citrus Resource Warehouse (crw.org.za)

harvestMonths.notes: Eureka is the dominant SA lemon cultivar ('accounting for about 85% of the planted hectares' per the same source). Same source states 'About half the lemons in South Africa is grown in the Eastern Cape, with the Limpopo province in second position. These two provinces together with the Western Cape account for 90% of lemon production.'

yearsToFirstCrop.notes: Source table lists 'First crop (years)' for Valencias / Navels / Grapefruit / Lemons as 4 / 4 / 3 / 3 respectively (single row, so column order is unambiguous); Lemons value is 3 years. 'Expected lifespan (years)' in the same table is given as 23 years for lemons.

yearsToFullBearing.notes: Not separately stated; source only gives 'first crop' age and overall expected orchard lifespan (23 years for lemons), not an age at full/mature bearing.

yieldKgPerTreeMature.notes: CONVERTED, arithmetic shown: the PDF table's text-extraction order groups three yield figures per crop column (interpreted as [potential/mature, likely, conservative] tons/ha, in the same crop order as the header row Valencias/Navels/Grapefruit/Lemons); this reconstruction of table alignment could not be double-checked against the original table grid, so it is a best-effort read, not a certainty. Using the 'likely production' figure for lemons (50 t/ha) and the source's own lemon spacings: hot areas '7.0-8.0 x 3.0-4.0m' (midpoint 7.5 x 3.5m = 26.25 m²/tree → 381 trees/ha → 50000kg / 381 = ~131 kg/tree) and cool/KZN-Midlands areas '5.5-6.0 x 2.5-3.0m' (midpoint 5.75 x 2.75m = 15.8 m²/tree → 632 trees/ha → 50000kg / 632 = ~79 kg/tree). Range [79,131] kg/tree reflects this spacing-driven spread, not cultivar variation. Editor review: table layout checked against the PDF (p.11). Each crop column lists Potential / Likely / Conservative from top to bottom, and the Lemons column reads 65 / 50 / 40 t/ha, so the read above is correct.

chillUnits.notes: Source gives 'HU' (heat units, base 13°C, accumulated to drive fruit maturity) of 1100-1500, not a classic winter chill-unit requirement. Citrus (evergreen) dormancy/flowering is driven more by cold-induced stress/heat-unit accumulation than by a chilling-hours model, and no source found stated an explicit 'no chill requirement' sentence for lemon, so the field is left null rather than converting HU into a chill-unit value; the HU figure is preserved here as the closest sourced analogue.

pollination.notes: Set to null in editor review: the quoted sentence ('they are very sour') says nothing about pollination; the value was a general-knowledge inference. Withdrawn value: self-fertile.

gaps: No verbatim, lemon-specific SA-source quote found stating a pollination requirement (self-fertile) — value entered from general citrus knowledge, not a directly sourced quote naming lemon; treat with caution.
No classic 'chill unit'/'chill hour' figure found for lemon (only a heat-unit, HU, figure) — left null.
